Observed data

Source: vignettes/observed-data.Rmd
observed-data.Rmd

Comparing a simulation against measured data is what turns a model run into a diagnostic. In esqlabsR, measured data is Observed Data: a named series of time/value points. It is the package’s term for what OSPS implements as a DataSet. This article covers how observed data enters a project, the four ways to declare a source, and how the project resolves that data when you build a figure.

It assumes you already know what a Project is and how to load one (see vignette("projects")). For turning observed data and simulated curves into figures, see vignette("plot-results"), which owns the plotting model; this article owns how the data gets into the project in the first place.

An observed-data source is a definition

A project does not store the measured numbers themselves. It stores a source definition: a small record under definitions/observed-data/<id>.json that says where the data comes from and how to read it. The actual DataSet is loaded on the fly from that definition whenever it is needed (at plot time, at validation time, or when you call loadObservedData() yourself), so the data is never baked into the project and always reflects the current source file.

There are four source types, distinguished only by where the data comes from:

  • excel reads one or more sheets of an Excel workbook through an OSPS data-importer configuration.
  • pkml reads a DataSet saved to a PKML file.
  • script sources an R script that builds and returns a DataSet (or several), recomputing the data from code each time it is resolved.
  • programmatic holds a DataSet you built in the current session; on save it is written to a PKML file so it survives a reload (see “Source type 4” below).

Throughout, scaffold a writable copy of the bundled example so the sources you add are written to a project you own, not the installed package:

project_dir <- withr::local_tempdir()
initProject(destination = project_dir, type = "example", createExcel = FALSE)
project <- loadProject(file.path(project_dir, "Project.json"))

The example already ships with one observed-data source, an Excel source. You can see it as a definition on the project:

project$definitions$observedData[[1]]
#> <ObservedDataSource>
#>   • Type: excel
#>   • File: Aciclovir_TimeValuesData.xlsx
#>   • Name: <empty string>
#>   • Importer Configuration: esqlabs_dataImporter_configuration.xml
#>   • Sheets: Laskin 1982.Group A

A note on observed-data ids

Two strings attach to every source, and they are not always equal, so keep them distinct:

  • The source id is the remove handle that removeObservedData() matches. It is taken verbatim (not canonicalized like other definitions): the declaration’s own id field when it sets one, and otherwise the file basename for an excel, pkml, or script source (for example Aciclovir_TimeValuesData.xlsx), or the DataSet name for a programmatic source.
  • The DataSet name is the reference handle that a DataCombined uses and getObservedDataNames() lists. It comes from the data itself: the Excel importer expands a sheet into a long, fully qualified name; a pkml or script source uses the DataSet$name.

Because the two can differ, read the DataSet name from getObservedDataNames() rather than typing it by hand.

Give a source an id when you want to choose that handle yourself instead of inheriting it from the file. The id also names the definition file, so the declaration below is stored as laskin_iv.json under the project’s observed-data definitions folder (definitions/observed-data/ in the default layout) rather than under the data file’s name:

addObservedData(
  project,
  list(
    id = "laskin_iv",
    type = "pkml",
    file = "laskin_1982_iv.pkml"
  )
)
removeObservedData(project, "laskin_iv")
getObservedDataNames(project)
#> [1] "Laskin 1982.Group A_Aciclovir_1_Human_MALE_PeripheralVenousBlood_Plasma_2.5 mg/kg_iv_"

Loading observed data

loadObservedData() resolves every declared source into a named list of DataSet objects, keyed by DataSet name. createDataCombined() (and therefore createPlots()) calls it internally to evaluate the observed side of a figure, so you rarely call it yourself.

observed <- loadObservedData(project)
names(observed)
#> [1] "Laskin 1982.Group A_Aciclovir_1_Human_MALE_PeripheralVenousBlood_Plasma_2.5 mg/kg_iv_"

getObservedDataNames() returns the same names without reloading (it caches after the first load), which is how you discover what a project knows before referencing it in a DataCombined.

Source type 1: Excel

An excel source names a workbook, an importer configuration, and the sheets to read. The bundled example’s source is exactly this. To add another, point at a file under the project’s data folder and supply the importer configuration and sheet names:

# shown but not run: the example already declares this exact source, and a
# duplicate file id aborts
addObservedData(
  project,
  list(
    type = "excel",
    file = "Aciclovir_TimeValuesData.xlsx",
    importerConfiguration = "esqlabs_dataImporter_configuration.xml",
    sheets = "Laskin 1982.Group A"
  )
)

The importer configuration is an OSPS data-importer XML that describes how the columns map to time, value, and metadata; the sheets field lists which sheets to import. The file paths are relative to the project’s data folder (project$paths$dataFolder).

Source type 2: PKML

A pkml source reads a DataSet that was saved to a PKML file. Here we build a small DataSet, save it into the project’s data folder as PKML, and declare it as a source:

data_folder <- project$paths$dataFolder

pkml_data <- ospsuite::DataSet$new(name = "Aciclovir extra cohort")
pkml_data$setValues(xValues = c(0, 1, 2, 4, 8), yValues = c(0, 9, 6, 3, 1))
pkml_data$xDimension <- ospsuite::ospDimensions$Time
pkml_data$yDimension <- ospsuite::ospDimensions$`Concentration (molar)`
ospsuite::saveDataSetToPKML(pkml_data, file.path(data_folder, "extra_cohort.pkml"))
#> NULL

addObservedData(project, list(type = "pkml", file = "extra_cohort.pkml"))
getObservedDataNames(project)
#> [1] "Laskin 1982.Group A_Aciclovir_1_Human_MALE_PeripheralVenousBlood_Plasma_2.5 mg/kg_iv_"
#> [2] "Aciclovir extra cohort"

The source definition is written to definitions/observed-data/extra_cohort.pkml.json; the PKML file stays under Data/, and the data is re-read from it whenever the project resolves observed data.

Source type 3: Script

A script source names an R script that the package sources at load time. The script must return a DataSet or a list of DataSet objects. The data is regenerated from code every time it is resolved, so a script source is the right choice when the data is computed (digitized points, a transformation of a raw file, a join across several inputs) rather than fixed: the recipe travels with the project and stays in step with its inputs. Write the script into the project (a scripts/ subfolder of the data folder keeps it tidy), then declare it:

script_dir <- file.path(data_folder, "scripts")
dir.create(script_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

writeLines(
  c(
    'ds <- ospsuite::DataSet$new(name = "Digitized literature curve")',
    "ds$setValues(xValues = c(0, 1, 2, 4, 8), yValues = c(0, 11, 8, 4, 2))",
    "ds$xDimension <- ospsuite::ospDimensions$Time",
    "ds$yDimension <- ospsuite::ospDimensions$`Concentration (molar)`",
    "ds"
  ),
  file.path(script_dir, "literature_curve.R")
)

addObservedData(project, list(type = "script", file = "scripts/literature_curve.R"))

The id of this source is the file basename, literature_curve.R, while the DataSet it produces is named Digitized literature curve (the name a DataCombined references). Because the script runs each time the data is resolved, anything you can compute in R (digitized points, a transformation of a raw file, a join across several inputs) becomes reproducible observed data.

Security. A script source runs the R file it names on your machine, with source(), whenever the data is resolved. Any R code in that file executes. Treat a project the way you would treat a script someone sends you: only load and resolve observed data from a project you trust. The first time a session sources a script source, the package warns you that this is happening.

Source type 4: Programmatic

addObservedData() also accepts a DataSet you have already built in the session. Build it in R and pass it directly:

scratch <- ospsuite::DataSet$new(name = "Scratch measurement")
scratch$setValues(xValues = c(0, 1, 3), yValues = c(0, 6, 2))

addObservedData(project, scratch)

Until you save, that DataSet lives on the in-memory project and the entry on disk is a {type: "programmatic", name} sentinel. On saveProject() the package writes the DataSet to a PKML file named after it (Scratch measurement.pkml) under the data folder and rewrites the entry to a pkml source. From then on it is an ordinary file-backed source: it survives a reload, and its remove id becomes the PKML file basename rather than the DataSet name.

Because saving turns a programmatic source into a pkml file, the data folder must be declared before you save; a project with no data folder cannot write the PKML and stops with a clear message. A programmatic sentinel that reaches a fresh session without its DataSet (a hand-authored declaration, or a project opened before it was ever saved) resolves to nothing, and the load warns you by name so it never vanishes silently.

Choosing between script and programmatic

Both survive a reload, so the choice is not about persistence:

  • Reach for programmatic (or pkml) for fixed measured data you already have. Nothing runs when the data is resolved: the values are read back from a file. This is the safe default.
  • Reach for script only when the data must be derived (recomputed from inputs each time), so the recipe stays in step with its inputs. The cost is that a script source executes arbitrary R when it is resolved (see the security note above), so use it only in a project you trust.

Removing a source

removeObservedData() takes the source id (the remove handle described above: the declaration’s own id when it sets one, and otherwise the file basename for an excel, pkml, or script source or the DataSet name for a programmatic one) and accepts a vector to remove several at once:

removeObservedData(project, c("extra_cohort.pkml", "Scratch measurement"))
getObservedDataNames(project)
#> [1] "Laskin 1982.Group A_Aciclovir_1_Human_MALE_PeripheralVenousBlood_Plasma_2.5 mg/kg_iv_"
#> [2] "Digitized literature curve"

If a removed source is still referenced by a DataCombined, the removal proceeds and leaves the reference dangling, which the next validateProject() (see vignette("validate-project")) reports as a problem, so prune the DataCombined too.

Where to go next

You now have all four ways observed data enters a project, and you know that the data is resolved on the fly from a source definition rather than stored in the project. To pair that observed data with simulated curves and turn it into report figures, see vignette("plot-results"). To check that every observed-data source and its references hang together, see vignette("validate-project").
